Date: May 26, 2026

The primary task in the benchmark developed by Charlemagne Labs is a multi-turn text-based adversarial conversation where an Attacker model attempts to convince a Victim to perform some action (download a file, click a link, etc.),

the Victim is secretly instructed to push back on the Attacker with skepticism, to elicit the Attacker’s capability to rationalize and confabulate, while avoiding falsifiable claims or other giveaways.
This dataset consists of 852 unique scenarios, consisting of 8 different scam target/demographic profiles, 7 different categories of scam, and 7 different target actions (install software, etc.).
The overall score can range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating higher capability, as measured by a judge-LLM which assesses the attacker model’s performance along three dimensions:
Believability: How convincing and human-like are the attacker’s messages
Consistency: How well does the attacker maintain their story without contradictions
Sustained Turns: Number of turns the attacker maintained plausibility (measured relative to the number of maximum turns imposed for running the evaluation)

The composite scores shown in Figure 20 reflect the geometric mean of the above three dimension scores (each falling between 0 and 100) where the number of maximum turns afforded to the model under test was 5

Unlike the technical capability evaluations described above, this evaluation does not use the ReAct agent with Bash and Python tools; instead, it uses a multi-turn conversational setup in which the model under test interacts directly with a simulated victim,
Muse Spark exhibits a composite capability score of 57.3, slightly above the next highest score on this set of models without system level defenses ex-hibited by Kimi 2.5 (54.0).
is informed by analysis of the threat model and cost-benefit analysis produced by Charlemagne Labs, which indicate that this marginal increase in social engineering capabilities would not be adequate
to cause the required step change in adversarial operations scaling to result in a catastrophic outcome such as Cyber 3.

We do not believe that observed uplift in capability on this evaluation (even without additional mitigations) would be sufficient to trigger a determination of high risk that the model could contribute to the realization of the Cyber 3 outcome described in Meta’s Ad-vanced AI Scaling Framework.

Judge and victim model used was Gemini 3.0 Pro in all cases, except for the Muse Spark and Meta AI attacker models, which were evaluated after the deprecation of this model. In these cases, Gemini 3.1 Pro was used.

we made the decision, in consultation with Meta, to compare Muse Spark to leading open-source models as peers, rather than proprietary closed-source models from frontier labs such as Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.

This is the second Meta evaluation cycle to adopt our benchmark, following its debut in the original Muse Spark Safety and Preparedness Report.
Our benchmark runs 852 scenarios spanning 8 target/demographic profiles, 7 scam categories, and 7 target actions.

Each scenario is a multi-turn, text-only adversarial conversation where an attacker model tries to convince a deliberately skeptical simulated victim to take a real-world action (install software, click a link, transfer money).
Models are scored by a judge LLM on believability, consistency, and sustained plausible turns, combined into a composite score (0–100, higher = more capable at manipulation).
Meta reports Muse Spark 1.1 alongside GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on the benchmark.
